778: \section{Dark matter-nucleon coupling}\label{app:dm-nucleon}
779: The dimensionful coupling between the mass eigenstates $(h,\,H)$ and pNG DM $\chi$ arises from eq.~\eqref{eqn:S_part}, namely
780: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:DM-h1-h2}
781: 	\lagr_S \supset - \left(\lambda_{\Phi S}\, \Phi^\dagger \Phi |S|^2 + \frac{\lambda_S}{2} |S|^4 \right).
782: \end{equation}
783: After EWSB, this term expands to (keeping only terms proportional to $\phi \chi^2$ and $s \chi^2$)
784: \begin{align*}
785: 	\lambda_{\Phi S} \, \Phi^\dagger \Phi |S|^2 &= \frac{\lambda_{\Phi S}}{4} (v_h + \phi)^2 \left[(v_s + s)^2 + \chi^2 \right] \supset \frac{\lambda_{\Phi S}}{4} (2 v_h \phi) \chi^2 = \frac{\lambda_{\Phi S} v_h}{2} \phi \chi^2, \\[1.5mm]
786: 	\frac{\lambda_S}{2} |S|^4 &= \frac{\lambda_S}{8} \left[ (v_s + s)^2 + \chi^2 \right]^2 \supset \frac{\lambda_S}{8} \left[2 (v_s + s)^2 \chi^2 \right] \supset \frac{\lambda_S}{8} (4 v_s s) \chi^2 = \frac{\lambda_S v_s}{2} s \chi^2.
787: \end{align*}
788: Thus, eq.~\eqref{eqn:DM-h1-h2} can be expressed as
789: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:DM-h-s}
790: 	\lagr_S \supset - \frac{1}{2} \chi^2 \left( \lambda_{\Phi S}  v_h \,\phi + \lambda_S v_s \,s \right).
791: \end{equation}
792: Using the following relation for the interaction eigenstates:
793: \begin{equation}
794: 	\begin{pmatrix}
795: 		\phi \\
796: 		s 
797: 	\end{pmatrix} = 
798: 	\begin{pmatrix}
799: 		\cos\theta & \sin\theta \\
800: 		-\sin\theta & \cos\theta
801: 	\end{pmatrix}
802: 	\begin{pmatrix}
803: 		h \\
804: 		H
805: 	\end{pmatrix},
806: \end{equation}
807: we can rewrite eq.~\eqref{eqn:DM-h-s} as
808: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:temp_DM_nucleon}
809: 	\lagr_S \supset - \frac{1}{2} \chi^2 (\kappa_{\chi \chi h} \, h + \kappa_{\chi \chi H} \, H),
810: \end{equation} 
811: where the \emph{dimensionful} couplings $\{\kappa_{\chi \chi h},\,\kappa_{\chi \chi H}\}$ are \cite{Gross:2017dan}
812: {\small
813:     \begin{align}
814: 	    \kappa_{\chi \chi h} = \left(\lambda_{\Phi S} v_h \cos\theta - \lambda_S v_s \sin\theta \right) &= \frac{1}{v_s} \left[ (m_H^2 - m_h^2) \sin \theta \cos^2 \theta - \sin\theta (m_h^2 \sin^2 \theta + m_H^2 \cos^2 \theta) \right] \nonumber \\
815: 	    &= - \frac{m_h^2}{v_s} \sin\theta, \\[1.5mm]
816: 	    \kappa_{\chi \chi H} = \left(\lambda_{\Phi S} v_h \sin\theta + \lambda_S v_s \cos\theta \right) &= \frac{1}{v_s} \left[(m_H^2 - m_h^2) \sin^2 \theta \cos \theta + \cos\theta (m_h^2 \sin^2 \theta + m_H^2 \cos^2 \theta) \right] \nonumber \\
817: 	    &= + \frac{m_H^2}{v_s} \cos\theta.
818:     \end{align}
819: }
820: On the other hand, the Yukawa interaction term in the SM Lagrangian reads
821: \begin{equation}
822: 	\lagr_{\textrm{Yukawa}} \supset - \phi \sum_f \frac{m_f}{v_h} \ovr{f} f = - \sum_f \kappa_{h f\ovr{f}} \, h \ovr{f} f + \kappa_{H f\ovr{f}} \, H \ovr{f} f,
823: \end{equation}
824: where 
825: \begin{equation}
826: 	\kappa_{h f\ovr{f}} = \frac{m_f}{v_h} \cos\theta, \quad \kappa_{H f\ovr{f}} = \frac{m_f}{v_h} \sin \theta,
827: \end{equation}
828: are the \emph{dimensionless} couplings between $h/H$ and SM quarks/leptons.~Finally, the pNG DM-nucleon interaction Lagrangian can be written as
829: \begin{equation}
830: 	\lagr_{\chi f} \supset - \frac{1}{2} \chi^2 (\kappa_{\chi \chi h} \, h + \kappa_{\chi \chi H} \, H) - \sum_f \kappa_{h f\ovr{f}} \, h \ovr{f} f + \kappa_{H f\ovr{f}} \, H \ovr{f} f.
831: \end{equation}
832: 
833: For a $\chi f \rightarrow \chi f$ scattering process via an $h/H$ exchange in $t$-channel, the tree-level direct detection (DD) scattering amplitude is proportional to
834: \begin{align*}
835: 	\mathcal{A}_{\textrm{DD}}(q^2) \propto \frac{\kappa_{\chi \chi h} \kappa_{h f\ovr{f}}}{q^2 - m_h^2} + \frac{\kappa_{\chi \chi H} \kappa_{H f\ovr{f}}}{q^2 - m_H^2} \propto \sin\theta \cos\theta \left(\frac{m_H^2}{q^2 - m_H^2} - \frac{m_h^2}{q^2 - m_h^2}\right),
836: \end{align*}
837: where $q \equiv \sqrt{2 M E}$ is the momentum transfer and $M$ is the nucleus mass.~In the limit of $q^2 \ll m_{h,H}^2$, the above expression becomes
838: \begin{equation}
839: 	\mathcal{A}_{\textrm{DD}}(q^2) \propto \sin\theta \cos\theta \left(\frac{1}{1 - q^2/m_h^2} - \frac{1}{1 - q^2/m_H^2}\right).
840: \end{equation}
841: For $x \ll 1$, the Taylor expansion for $(1 - x)^{-1} = 1 + x + \mathcal{O}(x^2)$. Thus, the above expression expands to
842: \begin{equation}
843: 	\mathcal{A}_{\textrm{DD}}(q^2) \propto q^2 \sin\theta \cos\theta \left(\frac{1}{m_h^2} - \frac{1}{m_H^2}\right).
844: \end{equation}
845: As $q \sim \mathcal{O}(10)$\,MeV, the pNG DM-nucleon cross section is momentum-suppressed at tree-level.
846: 
847: 
848: 
849: \section{The $S$, $T$ and $U$ parameters}\label{app:oblique_pars}
850: In our model, the oblique parameters are shifted from their SM values by \cite{Grimus:2008nb,Beniwal:2018hyi}
851: \begin{align}
852:     \Delta T &= \frac{3}{16\pi s_W^2} \left[\cos^2\theta \left \{f_T    \left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_W^2}\right) - \frac{1}{c_W^2}f_T\left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_Z^2}\right) \right\} + \sin^2\theta \left\{f_T\left(\frac{m_H^2}{m_W^2} \right) \right. \right. \nonumber \\
853:     &\hspace{4mm} \left. \left. - \frac{1}{c_W^2} f_T\left(\frac{m_H^2}{m_Z^2} \right) \right\} - \left\{f_T\left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_W^2}\right) - \frac{1}{c_W^2}f_T\left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_Z^2}\right) \right\} \right], \label{eqn:del_T} \\[1.5mm]
854:     \Delta S &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \left[\cos^2\theta f_S \left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_Z^2}\right) + \sin^2\theta f_S \left(\frac{m_H^2}{m_Z^2}\right) - f_S \left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_Z^2}\right) \right], \label{eqn:del_S} \\[1.5mm]    
855:     \Delta U &= \frac{1}{2\pi} \left[\cos^2\theta f_S \left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_W^2}\right) + \sin^2\theta f_S \left(\frac{m_H^2}{m_W^2}\right) - f_S \left(\frac{m_h^2}{m_W^2}\right) \right] - \Delta S, \label{eqn:del_U}
856: \end{align}
857: where $\Delta \mathcal{O} \equiv \mathcal{O} - \mathcal{O}_{\textnormal{SM}}$ for $\mathcal{O} \in (S, T, U)$, $m_W\,(m_Z)$ is the $W\,(Z)$ boson mass, $c_W^2 = m_W^2/m_Z^2$ and $s_W^2 = 1 - c_W^2$. The loop functions $f_T(x)$ and $f_S(x)$ are given by
858: \begin{align}
859:     f_T(x) &= \frac{x\log x}{x-1}, \\[1.5mm]
860:     f_S(x) &= 
861:     \begin{dcases}
862:         \frac{1}{12} \left[ -2 x^2 + 9 x + \left((x-3) \left(x^2-4 x+12\right)+\frac{1-x}{x}\right) f_T(x) \right. \\ 
863:         \left. + 2 \sqrt{(4-x) x} \left(x^2-4 x+12\right)    
864:         \tan ^{-1}\left(\sqrt{\frac{4 - x}{x}}\right) \right], \quad 0 < x < 4, \\
865:         \frac{1}{12} \left[-2 x^2 + 9 x + \left((x-3) \left(x^2-4 x+12\right)+\frac{1-x}{x}\right)f_T(x) \right. \\
866:         \left. + \sqrt{(x-4) x} \left(x^2 - 4x + 12\right)  \log \left( \frac{x - \sqrt{(x-4)x}}{x + \sqrt{(x-4)x}} \right)\right], \quad x \geq 4. 
867:     \end{dcases} 
868: \end{align}

710:   feynmangaugerules = If[Not[FeynmanGauge], {G0|GP|GPbar ->0}, {}];
711:  
712:   yuk = ExpandIndices[
713:    -yd[ff2, ff3] CKM[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].dR [sp, ff3, cc] Phi[ii] - 
714:     yl[ff1, ff3] LLbar[sp, ii, ff1].lR [sp, ff3] Phi[ii] -

717:   yuk+HC[yuk]/.feynmangaugerules
718:  ];

720: LGhost := Block[{LGh1,LGhw,LGhs,LGhphi,mu, generators,gh,ghbar,Vectorize,phi1,phi2,togoldstones,doublet,doublet0},
721:   (* Pure gauge piece *) 	
722:   LGh1 = -ghBbar.del[DC[ghB,mu],mu];
723:   LGhw = -ghWibar[ii].del[DC[ghWi[ii],mu],mu];
724:   LGhs = -ghGbar[ii].del[DC[ghG[ii],mu],mu];
725: 
726:   (* Scalar pieces: see Peskin pages 739-742 *)
727:   (* phi1 and phi2 are the real degrees of freedom of GP *)
728:   (* Vectorize transforms a doublet in a vector in the phi-basis, i.e. the basis of real degrees of freedom *)
729:   gh    = {ghB, ghWi[1], ghWi[2], ghWi[3]};
730:   ghbar = {ghBbar, ghWibar[1], ghWibar[2], ghWibar[3]};
731:   generators = {-I/2 g1 IdentityMatrix[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[1], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[3]};
732:   doublet = Expand[{(-I phi1 - phi2)/Sqrt[2], Phi[2]} /. MR$Definitions /. vev -> 0]; 
733:   doublet0 = {0, vev/Sqrt[2]};
734:   Vectorize[{a_, b_}]:= Simplify[{Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[b]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[b]]}/.{Im[_]->0, Re[num_]->num}];
735:   togoldstones := {phi1 -> (GP + GPbar)/Sqrt[2], phi2 -> (-GP + GPbar)/(I Sqrt[2])};
736:   LGhphi=Plus@@Flatten[Table[-ghbar[[kkk]].gh[[lll]] Vectorize[generators[[kkk]].doublet0].Vectorize[generators[[lll]].(doublet+doublet0)],{kkk,4},{lll,4}]] /.togoldstones;
737: 
738: ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];
739: 
740: LSM:= LGauge + LFermions + LHiggs + LYukawa + LGhost;

1: #!/usr/bin/env python3
2: """Deterministic lints for an agent-written FeynRules add-on (.fr) file.
3: 
4: Every rule encodes one construct that broke a compile, a FeynRules check or a
5: MadGraph import in the benchmark (prompt_addendum_v3.txt rules 9-15 and the
6: repair-loop taxonomy). A lint runs in milliseconds on the text; the compile it
7: predicts takes up to 900 s.
8: 
9: Each finding carries the STAGE it predicts:
10:   compile  - FeynRules will not load or will not finish the model
11:   checks   - the model loads but a consistency check fails
12:   mg5      - the UFO is written but MadGraph rejects it
13:   harness  - the validation harness cannot pick the total Lagrangian
14:   warn     - FeynRules warns; the run may still pass
15: 
16: Library: ``lint_text(text) -> list[Finding]``. CLI: ``fr_lint.py file.fr``.
17: """
18: 
19: from __future__ import annotations
20: 
21: import json
22: import re
23: import sys
24: from dataclasses import asdict, dataclass
25: from pathlib import Path
26: from typing import Dict, List, Optional, Set
27: 
28: HEPTAPOD = Path.home() / "Documents/Github/heptapod"
29: SM_FR = HEPTAPOD / "tools/feynrules/test_files/models/SM.fr"
30: 
31: # Mathematica built-ins and FeynRules symbols a class, parameter or index must
32: # not be named after (rule 10).
33: FR_SYMBOLS = {"HC", "CC", "FS", "DC", "del", "Eps", "Ga", "ProjP", "ProjM", "T",
34:               "Sig", "PauliSigma", "IndexDelta", "ME", "Index", "Indices", "Mass",
35:               "Width", "Value", "Unphysical", "Abelian"}
36: PROTECTED = {"N", "C", "D", "E", "I", "K", "O", "Pi", "Gamma", "Beta", "Zeta",
37:              "Sqrt", "Exp", "Log", "Sin", "Cos", "Tan", "Re", "Im", "Conjugate",
38:              "Sum", "Block", "Module", "Table", "If", "Which"}
39: 
40: # Names SM.fr declares: classes, class members, parameters, gauge groups, indices.
41: _SM_TEXT = SM_FR.read_text() if SM_FR.is_file() else ""
42: SM_CLASSES: Set[str] = set(re.findall(r"ClassName\s*->\s*(\w+)", _SM_TEXT))

62:                "Index", "Lorentz", "Spin", "Colour", "Gluon", "Generation",

64:                "Expand", "Simplify", "ProjPlus", "ProjMinus", "FR$", "vev"}

67: @dataclass
68: class Finding:
69:     rule: str
70:     stage: str  # compile | checks | mg5 | harness | warn
71:     message: str
72:     line: Optional[int] = None
73: 
74: 
75: # ------------------------------------------------------------------ parsing
76: 
77: def strip_comments(text: str) -> str:
78:     out, depth, i = [], 0, 0
79:     while i < len(text):
80:         if text.startswith("(*", i):
81:             depth += 1
82:             i += 2
83:             continue
84:         if text.startswith("*)", i) and depth:
85:             depth -= 1
86:             i += 2
87:             continue
88:         if depth == 0:
89:             out.append(text[i])
90:         elif text[i] == "\n":
91:             out.append("\n")
92:         i += 1
93:     return "".join(out)
94: 
95: 
96: def _matching(text: str, open_idx: int) -> int:
97:     depth = 0
98:     pairs = {"{": "}", "[": "]", "(": ")"}
99:     closes = set(pairs.values())
100:     for j in range(open_idx, len(text)):
101:         ch = text[j]
102:         if ch in pairs:
103:             depth += 1
104:         elif ch in closes:
105:             depth -= 1
106:             if depth == 0:
107:                 return j
108:     return len(text) - 1
109: 
110: 
111: def _block(text: str, name: str) -> str:
112:     m = re.search(rf"M\${name}\s*=\s*\{{", text)
113:     if not m:
114:         return ""
115:     end = _matching(text, m.end() - 1)
116:     return text[m.end():end]
117: 
118: 
119: def _entries(block: str) -> List[Dict]:
120:     """Top-level `Head == { ... }` entries of a M$ block."""
121:     out = []
122:     for m in re.finditer(r"(\w+(?:\[\s*\d+\s*\])?)\s*==\s*\{", block):
123:         end = _matching(block, m.end() - 1)
124:         body = block[m.end():end]
125:         out.append({"head": m.group(1), "body": body, "pos": m.start()})
126:     return out
127: 
128: 
129: def _prop(body: str, key: str) -> Optional[str]:
130:     m = re.search(rf"\b{key}\s*->\s*", body)
131:     if not m:
132:         return None
133:     rest = body[m.end():]
134:     if rest.startswith("{"):
135:         return rest[: _matching(rest, 0) + 1]
136:     mm = re.match(r"[^,}\n]+", rest)
137:     return mm.group(0).strip() if mm else None
138: 
139: 
140: def _is_kin_name(name: str) -> bool:
141:     return bool(re.search(r"kin|Kin|KIN|free|Free|Gauge|gauge", name))
142: 
143: 
144: def term_defs(text: str) -> List[Dict]:
145:     starts = [(m.group(1), m.start()) for m in re.finditer(r"^(L\w+)\s*:?=", text, re.M)]
146:     stops = [m.start() for m in re.finditer(r"^(?:M\$\w+\s*=|L\w+\s*:?=|\w+\s*=\s*\{)", text, re.M)]
147:     out = []
148:     for name, s in starts:
149:         e = min([x for x in stops if x > s] + [len(text)])
150:         out.append({"name": name, "body": text[s:e], "line": text[:s].count("\n") + 1})
151:     return out
152: 
153: 
154: def _line_of(text: str, needle: str) -> Optional[int]:
155:     i = text.find(needle)
156:     return text[:i].count("\n") + 1 if i >= 0 else None
157: 
158: 
159: # -------------------------------------------------------------------- lints
160: 
161: def lint_text(raw: str) -> List[Finding]:
162:     text = strip_comments(raw)
163:     F: List[Finding] = []
164:     classes = _entries(_block(text, "ClassesDescription"))
165:     params = _entries(_block(text, "Parameters"))
166:     terms = term_defs(text)
167:     term_names = {t["name"] for t in terms}
168:     term_bodies = "\n".join(t["body"] for t in terms)
169: 
170:     class_names, class_idx = {}, {}
171:     for c in classes:
172:         cn = _prop(c["body"], "ClassName")
173:         if cn:
174:             class_names[cn] = c
175:             mi = re.match(r"(\w+)\[\s*(\d+)\s*\]", c["head"])
176:             if mi:
177:                 class_idx[cn] = (mi.group(1), int(mi.group(2)))
178:     param_names = {p["head"]: p for p in params}
179:     index_decls = dict(re.findall(r"IndexRange\[\s*Index\[(\w+)\]\s*\]\s*=\s*([^;\n]+)", text))
180: 
181:     # --- rule 10: names -------------------------------------------------
182:     for name in list(class_names) + list(param_names) + list(index_decls):
183:         if name in FR_SYMBOLS:
184:             F.append(Finding("feynrules_symbol_name", "compile",
185:                              f"`{name}` is a FeynRules symbol", _line_of(text, name)))
186:         elif name in PROTECTED:
187:             F.append(Finding("protected_name", "warn",
188:                              f"`{name}` is a Mathematica built-in (loads with a warning; renaming is safer)",
189:                              _line_of(text, name)))
190:     for name in class_names:
191:         if name in SM_CLASSES or name in SM_MEMBERS:
192:             F.append(Finding("sm_class_redeclared", "warn",
193:                              f"class `{name}` is already declared by SM.fr (doubly-defined class)",
194:                              _line_of(text, f"ClassName -> {name}")))
195:     for name in param_names:
196:         if name in SM_PARAMS or name in SM_MASSES:
197:             F.append(Finding("sm_parameter_redeclared", "warn",
198:                              f"parameter `{name}` is already declared by SM.fr", _line_of(text, name)))
199:     for cn, c in class_names.items():
200:         for key in ("ParticleName", "AntiParticleName"):
201:             v = _prop(c["body"], key)
202:             names = re.findall(r'"([^"]*)"', v) if v else []
203:             if v and any(re.search(r"[\'`\s!@#%^&*()=\[\]{}|\\;:<>?/,]", nm) for nm in names):
204:                 F.append(Finding("bad_particle_name", "mg5",
205:                                  f"class `{cn}`: {key} {v} is not a valid UFO identifier", _line_of(text, v)))
206:         if cn in class_idx and class_idx[cn][1] < 100:
207:             F.append(Finding("low_class_index", "warn",
208:                              f"class `{cn}` uses index {class_idx[cn][0]}[{class_idx[cn][1]}]; SM.fr uses the low indices",
209:                              _line_of(text, c["head"])))
210:         for m in re.finditer(r"ClassMembers\s*->\s*\{([^}]*)\}", c["body"]):
211:             for mem in [x.strip() for x in m.group(1).split(",") if x.strip()]:

219:                 F.append(Finding("dollar_in_name", "mg5", f"`{m.group(0)}` contains `$` (invalid Python)",
220:                                  text[:m.start()].count("\n") + 1))
221:                 break
222: 
223:     # --- rule 11: interaction orders --------------------------------------
224:     hierarchy = _block(text, "InteractionOrderHierarchy")
225:     orders_declared = set(re.findall(r"\{\s*(\w+)\s*,\s*-?\d+\s*\}", hierarchy))
226:     for pn, p in param_names.items():
227:         body = p["body"]
228:         ptype = (_prop(body, "ParameterType") or "External").strip()
229:         io = _prop(body, "InteractionOrder")
230:         used = re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(pn)}\b", term_bodies) is not None

233:                       for c in classes) or re.match(r"^(M|W)[A-Z]", pn) and not io

239:                                      f"parameter `{pn}` uses InteractionOrder `{o}` not listed in M$InteractionOrderHierarchy",
240:                                      _line_of(text, pn)))
241:     ordered = {pn for pn, p in param_names.items() if _prop(p["body"], "InteractionOrder")}
242:     internal = {pn for pn, p in param_names.items()
243:                 if (_prop(p["body"], "ParameterType") or "External").strip() == "Internal"}
244:     # an Internal parameter inherits the orders of the parameters in its Value

254:         if used_params and not (used_params & ordered) and not \
255:                 any(re.search(rf"\b{c}\b", t["body"]) for c in sm_couplings) and \
256:                 not any(re.search(rf"\b(DC|FS)\[", t["body"]) for _ in [0]):
257:             F.append(Finding("missing_interaction_order", "mg5",
258:                              f"`{t['name']}`: none of its parameters ({', '.join(sorted(used_params))}) carries an InteractionOrder",

261:     # --- rule 12: pattern rules on tensor parameters -----------------------

284:                                  f"`{t['name']}`: covariant derivative on an explicitly indexed field `{fld}`", t["line"]))

286:         if re.search(r"Index\[\s*Generation\s*,\s*\w+\s*\]\s*,\s*Index\[\s*Generation", b) or \
287:                 re.search(r"\w+\[\s*Generation\s*,\s*\w+\s*\]", b):

289:                              f"`{t['name']}`: nested generation index", t["line"]))

334:                 continue

338:                 for hit in pat.finditer(t["body"]):
339:                     if not re.search(r"1/2|0\.5", hit.group(1)):

342:                                          t["line"]))
343:     # undeclared symbols in terms (conservative: capitalised identifiers used as fields)
344:     declared = set(class_names) | {c + "bar" for c in class_names} | set(param_names) | \
345:         SM_FIELDS_ALL | SM_PARAMS | SM_MASSES | FR_BUILTINS | set(term_names) | set(index_decls) | \

347:          "Cot", "Abs", "MatrixExp", "DiagonalMatrix", "IdentityMatrix", "Sum", "Product"}
348:     for c in classes:
349:         for key in ("Mass", "Width"):
350:             v = _prop(c["body"], key) or ""
351:             declared |= set(re.findall(r"\b([A-Za-z]\w*)\b", v)) - {"Internal", "External", "Automatic"}
352:     for c in classes:
353:         for m in re.finditer(r"ClassMembers\s*->\s*\{([^}]*)\}", c["body"]):
354:             for mem in [x.strip() for x in m.group(1).split(",") if x.strip()]:
355:                 declared |= {mem, mem + "bar"}
356:         for m in re.finditer(r"Unphysical\s*->\s*True", c["body"]):
357:             pass
358:     for t in terms:
359:         b = re.sub(r'"[^"]*"', "", t["body"])
360:         locals_ = set()
361:         for m in re.finditer(r"(?:Block|Module)\[\s*\{([^}]*)\}", b):
362:             locals_ |= {x.strip().split("=")[0].strip() for x in m.group(1).split(",")}
363:         for m in re.finditer(r"\b([A-Za-z]\w*)\b", b):
364:             s = m.group(1)
365:             if s in declared or s in locals_ or s == t["name"] or len(s) < 2:

367:             if re.match(r"^(mu|nu|rho|sig|la|lam|al|be|sp|ss|ii|jj|kk|ll|ff|gg|cc|aa|bb|tt|rr|xx|yy|zz)\d*$", s):

369:             if s in ("ExpandIndices", "FlavorExpand", "Index", "Sqrt", "HC"):
370:                 continue
371:             if s[0].isupper() and re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(s)}\s*[\[.]", b):
372:                 F.append(Finding("undeclared_symbol", "warn",
373:                                  f"`{t['name']}` uses `{s}` which is neither declared here nor by SM.fr",
374:                                  t["line"]))

377:     # --- rule 9: non-fundamental colour representations -----------------------
378:     for iname, rng in index_decls.items():

383:     # --- mass mixing written into Definitions (the dominant check failure) ----
384:     phys_new = {cn for cn, c in class_names.items() if (_prop(c["body"], "Unphysical") or "").strip() != "True"}
385:     for cn, c in class_names.items():
386:         d = _prop(c["body"], "Definitions") or ""
387:         if not d:
388:             continue
389:         fields_in = {s for s in re.findall(r"\b([A-Za-z]\w*)\b", d) if s in phys_new or s in SM_CLASSES}
390:         fields_in -= {cn}
391:         if len(fields_in) >= 2 and re.search(r"\b(sa|ca|sin|cos|Sin|Cos|s\w*|c\w*)\w*\b", d):
392:             F.append(Finding("mixing_in_definitions", "checks",
393:                              f"class `{cn}` is defined as a mixture of {sorted(fields_in)}; the mass basis of the partner fields declared in SM.fr is unchanged",
394:                              _line_of(text, f"ClassName -> {cn}")))
395:     return F
396: 
397: 
398: def lint_file(path: str) -> List[Finding]:
399:     return lint_text(Path(path).read_text(errors="replace"))
400: 
401: 
402: if __name__ == "__main__":
403:     for p in sys.argv[1:]:
404:         fs = lint_file(p)
405:         print(json.dumps({"file": p, "findings": [asdict(f) for f in fs]}, indent=1))

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Deterministic lints for an agent-written FeynRules add-on (.fr) file.

Every rule encodes one construct that broke a compile, a FeynRules check or a
MadGraph import in the benchmark (prompt_addendum_v3.txt rules 9-15 and the
repair-loop taxonomy). A lint runs in milliseconds on the text; the compile it
predicts takes up to 900 s.

Each finding carries the STAGE it predicts:
  compile  - FeynRules will not load or will not finish the model
  checks   - the model loads but a consistency check fails
  mg5      - the UFO is written but MadGraph rejects it
  harness  - the validation harness cannot pick the total Lagrangian
  warn     - FeynRules warns; the run may still pass

Library: ``lint_text(text) -> list[Finding]``. CLI: ``fr_lint.py file.fr``.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

## Important Details
- Working dir: `/private/var/folders/pf/fm0v0g_52r754cfv3r4lqv980000gn/T/ob-pNG-2hdjbans/` — work only inside it.

OUTPUT: write the FeynRulesModel JSON object to spec.json in the current directory with your file-writing tool (ONLY the JSON). Set model_name to "pNG_gen". Run `./frgen spec.json` and iterate as described under TOOLKIT. Your final message: the self-audit table and one line with the last ./frgen result. spec.json as it is on disk when you stop is rendered and scored.

SANDBOX: the current directory contains ONLY the paper (paper/1912.04008_source.tex), SM.fr (the Standard
Model file this add-on is loaded on top of: take field names, index conventions and
hypercharges from it), the schema tools/frgen/frmodel.py, the renderer
tools/frgen/render.py, the lints tools/fr_lint.py and the command ./frgen. Nothing else
exists here and nothing outside this directory may be read. You have file read, search and
write tools, and ONE shell command: `./frgen spec.json`. No other shell command, no web,
no FeynRules, no Mathematica and no MadGraph.

TOOLKIT: `./frgen spec.json` (1) validates spec.json against the FeynRulesModel schema and
prints every schema error, (2) renders model.fr with the deterministic renderer, and (3)
lints model.fr with deterministic rules, each tagged with the stage it predicts will fail.
Run it after you write spec.json, fix what it reports, and run it again until the schema
is OK and every remaining lint finding is one you have checked and judged harmless.

AUTOMATIC CHECK: after every write or edit of spec.json the toolkit runs by itself and
its report is appended to that tool's result. Read it after each change and fix what it
reports. You may still run `./frgen spec.json` yourself.

## Physics-completeness rules (apply to every model)

1. Free-field terms for every new particle class. Write a named kinetic + mass term for each new field even when the paper shows only L_int. Use the mass symbol declared in the class `Mass -> {M, value}`. Add the term to the total Lagrangian sum.
   - Real vector (gauge singlet): `LXkin := -1/4 FS[X, mu, nu] FS[X, mu, nu] + 1/2 MX^2 X[mu] X[mu];` (the explicit form `-1/4 (del[X[nu], mu] - del[X[mu], nu])^2` is equivalent).
   - Complex vector: `-1/2 FS[Xbar, mu, nu] FS[X, mu, nu] + MX^2 Xbar[mu] X[mu]`.
   - Complex scalar: `DC[phibar, mu] DC[phi, mu] - Mphi^2 phibar phi`. Real scalar: `1/2 del[phi, mu] del[phi, mu] - 1/2 Mphi^2 phi^2`.
   - Dirac fermion: `I psibar.Ga[mu].DC[psi, mu] - Mpsi psibar.psi`. Majorana fermion (`SelfConjugate -> True`): `I/2 psibar.Ga[mu].del[psi, mu] - 1/2 Mpsi psibar.psi`.

2. Explicit EFT cutoffs. When the paper writes an operator with `1/Lambda^n` (or `1/M^n`, `1/f^n`), declare each distinct cutoff as an External parameter in GeV with the paper's benchmark value, e.g. `Lam == { ParameterType -> External, Value -> 1000., BlockName -> CUTOFF, InteractionOrder -> {QED, -1}, Description -> "EFT cutoff [GeV], Eq.(N)" }`. Write the factor `1/Lam^(d-4)` verbatim in the term, with `d` the operator mass dimension you computed in the self-audit. Keep the paper's dimensionless couplings (kappa, lambda, c_i) dimensionless with the paper's benchmark defaults. Do this for the term and for its `HC[...]` partner. Only if the paper's own implementation absorbs `kappa/Lambda^n` into one coefficient may you do the same; then the parameter Description must say "= kappa/Lambda^n, mass dimension -n, units GeV^-n" and the default must equal the paper's numeric `kappa/Lambda^n`. Never leave a dimensionful coefficient with an unexplained O(0.1) default.

3. Charge conjugation. When the paper writes a fermion with a charge-conjugation superscript (`psi^c`, `\bar{psi^c}`, `psi^T C`, or a Majorana mass eigenstate that enters a chiral current with the opposite chirality), write it as `CC[psi]` (and `bar[CC[psi]]` for the conjugated bar). Never write the bare field. If the paper's benchmark sets that term's coefficient to zero, either drop the term or write it with `CC[...]`; never keep the term with the conjugation dropped. Use the class field with its Generation index (for example the SM class `vl[ff]`), not a class member like `ve[nn]`, because FeynRules reads an index on a class member as a spin index.

4. SU(2) doublet contractions. Use the SM.fr conventions the add-on loads on: `Phi` has Y = +1/2, `LL` has Y = -1/2, `QL` has Y = +1/6, `Phi[1] = -I GP`, `Phi[2] = (vev + H + I G0)/Sqrt[2]`. Contract a doublet with an anti-doublet on a shared index: `LLbar[sp, ii, ff] ... Phi[ii]`. Contract two objects of the same conjugation type (`LLbar` with `Phibar`, `QLbar` with `Phibar`, i.e. any term the paper writes with `Htilde = i tau2 H*`) with `Eps[ii, jj]` on two distinct indices: `LLbar[sp, ii, ff] ... Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj]`. Never contract `LLbar[ii]` with `Phibar[ii]`. Model the SM Yukawas: `QLbar.dR Phi[ii]`, `LLbar.lR Phi[ii]`, `QLbar.uR Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj]`.

5. New U(1) charges. Do not copy a paper's charge table literally when the paper's Yukawa equation and its table use different hypercharge conventions (for example the paper effectively uses Y(H) = -1/2). Re-derive the new-U(1) charge of every SM field, including the Higgs, from the requirement that all SM Yukawas and all new Yukawas are invariant under SM.fr conventions. Report which sign you chose and why. Do not put quantum numbers on a `SelfConjugate -> True` class; put a chiral charge on an Unphysical chiral class instead.

6. Read only the paper. Do not open any cached or reference `.fr` file for the same model. If you see one, say so in the output and do not use it.

7. Fractions and roots in extracted equations. The paper text is machine-extracted. A displayed fraction or radical can arrive flattened: the numerator, the fraction bar and the denominator become separate lines, so `A / Sqrt[B]` and `A Sqrt[B]` look identical. For every coefficient that contains a fraction, a square root or a power:
   - If a LaTeX source file (`*_source.tex`) is available, read the `\frac{...}{...}` and `\sqrt{...}` there and take it literally. The LaTeX is authoritative over the flattened text.
   - Otherwise cross-check the placement against a second equation of the paper that depends on the same coefficient (a partial width, a cross section, a limit, or a small-parameter expansion) and name that equation in the self-audit. A coupling `g/Sqrt[1-x]` gives a width proportional to `1/(1-x)`; a coupling `g Sqrt[1-x]` gives a width proportional to `(1-x)`.
   - If neither resolves it, choose the form that reproduces a numerical value the paper states, and say so.
   Never silently pick one placement.

8. Mass mixing. When the paper diagonalises a mass mixing between a new state and an SM state (Z-Z', h-S, W-W_R, nu-N), write the mass eigenstates the paper uses: declare the mixing angle (External, or Internal with the paper's formula) and express the gauge eigenstates through it in `Definitions` of Unphysical classes. Do not leave the mixing in a comment.

## FeynRules and UFO construct rules (each one broke a compile or a MadGraph import in earlier runs)

9. Non-fundamental colour representations. If a field carries a colour index other than the triplet `Colour` or the adjoint `Gluon` (for example a sextet), declare the index range AND add the representation line FeynRules needs, before the field declarations: `AddGaugeRepresentation[SU3C -> {T6, Sextet}];` for a sextet (schema: put both lines in `raw_preamble`; also keep the `index_decls` entry). Write covariant derivatives on the whole field, `DC[Phi, mu]`, never with an explicit colour index inside `DC[...]`.

10. Names. Class names, parameter names and index names must not be Mathematica built-ins or FeynRules symbols: never `N`, `C`, `D`, `E`, `I`, `K`, `O`, `HC`, `CC`, `FS`, `DC`, `del`, `Eps`, `Ga`, `ProjP`, `ProjM`, and never a name SM.fr already declares (`H`, `Phi`, `Z`, `W`, `A`, `G`, `ee`, `gs`, `gw`, `sw`, `cw`, `vev`, `MZ`, `MW`, ...). No primes or punctuation in `ParticleName`/`AntiParticleName` (`W'` is not a valid UFO name; write `Wp`, `Wpbar`). Use class indices of 100 or more for new classes.

11. Interaction orders. Every new coupling parameter (Yukawa, portal, quartic, new gauge coupling, dimensionless EFT coefficient) carries an `InteractionOrder`: `{NP, 1}` for a new-physics coupling, `{QED, 1}` or `{QCD, 1}` only when it is literally that coupling. Declare `M$InteractionOrderHierarchy` with every order you use (for example `{{QCD, 1}, {QED, 2}, {NP, 1}}`). A coupling with no order makes MadGraph reject the UFO ("Some couplings have '1' order").

12. Tensor parameters. Give every indexed parameter explicit per-component values (`yN[1,1] -> 0.1, yN[1,2] -> 0, ...`; schema: `value_rules`). Never use a pattern rule such as `X[i_?NumericQ, j_?NumericQ] :> ...` in `Definitions`: FeynRules exports the pattern verbatim as a UFO parameter name and MadGraph fails with an unrelated "invalid syntax" error.

13. Flavour structure in matrix form. Write generation-space couplings as matrix products between class fields, `uqbar.VCKMR.Ga[mu].ProjP.dq`, `LLbar.yN.NR`, `ISbar.Ga[mu].ProjM.IS`, not as explicit index sums `VCKMR[ff1, ff2] uqbar[ff1, cc]...dq[ff2, cc]`, and never nest one generation index inside another. Explicit-index forms leak FeynRules internals (`ConvertSpinToString`, `MakeIdenticalFermions`) into the UFO.

14. One declared total. Define exactly one Lagrangian term named `LTotal` that sums every other term you define, and make sure every other term appears in that sum. Do not define two alternative totals. Do not emit a term that contains no field (a pure constant): FeynRules exports it as a vertex with no particles.

15. Declarations. Every field used in a term is declared; every parameter used in a term is declared with a numeric default; every `SelfConjugate -> True` class has no `QuantumNumbers`; a Majorana mass term is `-1/2 M psibar.psi`.

## Mandatory self-audit table (produce it BEFORE the model)

For every Lagrangian term you emit, output one row of this table. Then fix any row that fails before you write the model.

| term name | fields in the monomial | operator mass dimension d | coupling symbol | coupling mass dimension (must be 4 - d) | 1/Lambda power present (must be d - 4, or "n/a" if d <= 4) | Q sum | Y sum | SU(2) contraction (singlet? which Eps or shared index) | SU(3) contraction | sum of each new U(1) charge (one column per U(1), must be 0) | lepton/baryon number sum (if the paper assigns them) | CC[] used where paper writes psi^c (yes/no/n/a) | fraction/root placement checked against (equation, LaTeX line, or "n/a") | Hermitian partner (HC[] or self-conjugate) |

Rules for the table:
- Field mass dimensions: scalar 1, vector 1, fermion 3/2, `FS[...]` 2, `del`/`DC` 1.
- Every Q sum, Y sum, and new-U(1) sum must equal 0. Use the charges you declared in `QuantumNumbers` and the SM.fr charges for SM fields. If a sum is not 0, the term is wrong; fix the contraction or the charge before you continue.
- If d > 4, the row must show `1/Lambda^(d-4)` and an External cutoff parameter, or a Description that states the absorbed dimension and units.
- Add one row per new particle class that confirms its kinetic + mass term exists and is in the total Lagrangian sum.
- Add one row per non-fundamental colour representation that confirms the `AddGaugeRepresentation[...]` line is present.
- Add one line under the table that lists every `SelfConjugate -> True` class and confirms it carries no `QuantumNumbers`.
- Add one line that lists every class, parameter and index name you chose and confirms none is a Mathematica built-in, a FeynRules symbol, or an SM.fr name.
- Add one line that names the single total Lagrangian and lists the terms it sums.
- Add one line that states whether any reference or cached model file was read (must be "none").

28: # A verbatim numeric string: "-1/3", "1500.", "2.5*^-3", "Internal", "Automatic".
29: NumberStr = str

31: _OPEN = {"(": ")", "[": "]", "{": "}"}
32: _CLOSE = {v: k for k, v in _OPEN.items()}

35: def unbalanced(text: str) -> Optional[str]:
36:     """Why ``text`` has unbalanced brackets, or None when it is balanced.
37: 
38:     Mathematica strings ("...") and comments ((* ... *), nested) are skipped. An
39:     unbalanced verbatim string renders into a .fr that FeynRules stops reading
40:     with "Unexpected end of file" or "Invalid syntax", long after the schema
41:     said OK.
42:     """
43:     stack: List[Tuple[str, int]] = []
44:     i, n, depth = 0, len(text), 0
45:     while i < n:
46:         c = text[i]
47:         if depth:                                  # inside a comment
48:             if text.startswith("(*", i):
49:                 depth, i = depth + 1, i + 2
50:             elif text.startswith("*)", i):
51:                 depth, i = depth - 1, i + 2
52:             else:
53:                 i += 1
54:             continue
55:         if text.startswith("(*", i):
56:             depth, i = 1, i + 2
57:             continue
58:         if c == '"':                               # string literal
59:             i += 1
60:             while i < n and text[i] != '"':
61:                 i += 2 if text[i] == "\\" else 1
62:             if i >= n:
63:                 return "unterminated string literal"
64:             i += 1
65:             continue
66:         if c in _OPEN:
67:             stack.append((c, i))
68:         elif c in _CLOSE:
69:             if not stack or stack[-1][0] != _CLOSE[c]:
70:                 ctx = text[max(0, i - 30):i + 1]
71:                 return f"unexpected '{c}' at character {i} (...{ctx})"
72:             stack.pop()
73:         i += 1
74:     if depth:
75:         return "unterminated comment"
76:     if stack:
77:         c, j = stack[-1]
78:         ctx = text[j:j + 30]
79:         return f"'{c}' at character {j} is never closed ({ctx}...)"
80:     return None

404: def topo_sort_parameters(params: List[Parameter]) -> List[Parameter]:

478:                         "name twice. Give one of them its own block_name (or, for "
479:                         "scalars, its own order_block)"

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Deterministic lints for an agent-written FeynRules add-on (.fr) file.

Every rule encodes one construct that broke a compile, a FeynRules check or a
MadGraph import in the benchmark (prompt_addendum_v3.txt rules 9-15 and the
repair-loop taxonomy). A lint runs in milliseconds on the text; the compile it
predicts takes up to 900 s.

Each finding carries the STAGE it predicts:
  compile  - FeynRules will not load or will not finish the model
  checks   - the model loads but a consistency check fails
  mg5      - the UFO is written but MadGraph rejects it
  harness  - the validation harness cannot pick the total Lagrangian
  warn     - FeynRules warns; the run may still pass

Library: ``lint_text(text) -> list[Finding]``. CLI: ``fr_lint.py file.fr``.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

264:         (

267:         ),
268:         ("Indices", _indices(p.indices) if p.indices else None),
269:         ("FlavorIndex", p.flavor_index),
270:         ("Mass", _mass(p.mass) if p.mass else None),
271:         ("Width", _mass(p.width) if p.width else None),
272:         ("QuantumNumbers",
273:          _qn(p.quantum_numbers) if _additive_qns(p.quantum_numbers or {}) else None),
274:         ("PDG", _pdg(p.pdg) if p.pdg is not None else None),
275:         ("ParticleName", _name_field(p.particle_name) if p.particle_name else None),
276:         (

291:         (

295:         ("Unphysical", _bool(True) if p.unphysical else None),
296:         (

309: def render_model(model: FeynRulesModel) -> str:
310:     """Render a validated FeynRulesModel to a complete ``.fr`` string."""
311:     sections: List[str] = [render_information(model.info)]

313:     if model.interaction_order_hierarchy:
314:         ih = ", ".join(_interaction_order(t) for t in model.interaction_order_hierarchy)

316:     if model.interaction_order_limit:
317:         il = ", ".join(_interaction_order(t) for t in model.interaction_order_limit)
318:         sections.append("M$InteractionOrderLimit = {" + il + "};")
319:     if model.feynman_gauge is not None:
320:         sections.append(f"FeynmanGauge = {_bool(model.feynman_gauge)};")
321:     if model.vevs:
322:         vv = ", ".join(f"{{{f}, {v}}}" for f, v in model.vevs)
323:         sections.append("M$vevs = {" + vv + "};")
324: 
325:     for raw in model.raw_preamble:

328:     if model.index_decls:
329:         sections.append(render_index_decls(model.index_decls))
330:     if model.gauge_groups:
331:         sections.append(render_gauge_groups(model.gauge_groups))
332:     if model.parameters:
333:         # FeynRules auto-declares the mass/width parameters named in each
334:         # particle's Mass/Width spec. Re-declaring them in M$Parameters makes the
335:         # UFO define the name twice, which MadGraph rejects ("name X define
336:         # multiple time"). Drop those duplicates; keep genuine couplings.
337:         reserved = _reserved_mass_width_names(model.particles)
338:         params = [p for p in model.parameters
339:                   if p.name not in reserved or _is_internal_param(p)]
340:         if params:
341:             sections.append(render_parameters(params))
342:     if model.particles:
343:         sections.append(render_classes(model.particles))
344:     for field, expr in model.gauge_xi:
345:         sections.append(f"GaugeXi[{field}] = {expr};")
346: 
347:     for raw in model.raw_blocks:
348:         sections.append(raw)
349: 
350:     for t in model.lagrangian_terms:
351:         op = ":=" if t.delayed else "="
352:         # Defensive: some (LLM-produced) expressions already carry a leading
353:         # assignment operator ("= ..." or ":= ..."); strip it so we don't emit a
354:         # duplicated operator (e.g. "L := := Block[...]").
355:         rhs = t.expression.lstrip()
356:         for lead in (":=", "="):
357:             if rhs.startswith(lead):
358:                 rhs = rhs[len(lead):].lstrip()
359:                 break
360:         sections.append(f"{t.name} {op} {rhs};")
361: 
362:     env = Environment(
363:         loader=FileSystemLoader(_TEMPLATE_DIR),
364:         autoescape=select_autoescape(enabled_extensions=(), default=False),
365:         keep_trailing_newline=True,
366:     )
367:     template = env.get_template("model.fr.j2")
368:     return template.render(model_name=model.model_name, body="\n\n".join(sections))

717:   yuk+HC[yuk]/.feynmangaugerules
718:  ];

722:   LGh1 = -ghBbar.del[DC[ghB,mu],mu];
723:   LGhw = -ghWibar[ii].del[DC[ghWi[ii],mu],mu];
724:   LGhs = -ghGbar[ii].del[DC[ghG[ii],mu],mu];

727:   (* phi1 and phi2 are the real degrees of freedom of GP *)
728:   (* Vectorize transforms a doublet in a vector in the phi-basis, i.e. the basis of real degrees of freedom *)
729:   gh    = {ghB, ghWi[1], ghWi[2], ghWi[3]};
730:   ghbar = {ghBbar, ghWibar[1], ghWibar[2], ghWibar[3]};

734:   Vectorize[{a_, b_}]:= Simplify[{Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[b]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[b]]}/.{Im[_]->0, Re[num_]->num}];

737: 
738: ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];
739: 
740: LSM:= LGauge + LFermions + LHiggs + LYukawa + LGhost;

(* *****   Lagrangian   ***** *)
(* ************************** *)

LGauge := Block[{mu,nu,ii,aa}, 
  ExpandIndices[-1/4 FS[B,mu,nu] FS[B,mu,nu] - 1/4 FS[Wi,mu,nu,ii] FS[Wi,mu,nu,ii] - 1/4 FS[G,mu,nu,aa] FS[G,mu,nu,aa], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];

LFermions := Block[{mu}, 
  ExpandIndices[I*(
    QLbar.Ga[mu].DC[QL, mu] + LLbar.Ga[mu].DC[LL, mu] + uRbar.Ga[mu].DC[uR, mu] + dRbar.Ga[mu].DC[dR, mu] + lRbar.Ga[mu].DC[lR, mu]), 
  FlavorExpand->{SU2W,SU2D}]/.{CKM[a_,b_] Conjugate[CKM[a_,c_]]->IndexDelta[b,c], CKM[b_,a_] Conjugate[CKM[c_,a_]]->IndexDelta[b,c]}];

LHiggs := Block[{ii,mu, feynmangaugerules},
  feynmangaugerules = If[Not[FeynmanGauge], {G0|GP|GPbar ->0}, {}];
 
  ExpandIndices[DC[Phibar[ii],mu] DC[Phi[ii],mu] + muH^2 Phibar[ii] Phi[ii] - lam Phibar[ii] Phi[ii] Phibar[jj] Phi[jj], FlavorExpand->{SU2D,SU2W}]/.feynmangaugerules
 ];

LYukawa := Block[{sp,ii,jj,cc,ff1,ff2,ff3,yuk,feynmangaugerules},
  feynmangaugerules = If[Not[FeynmanGauge], {G0|GP|GPbar ->0}, {}];
 
  yuk = ExpandIndices[
   -yd[ff2, ff3] CKM[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].dR [sp, ff3, cc] Phi[ii] - 
    yl[ff1, ff3] LLbar[sp, ii, ff1].lR [sp, ff3] Phi[ii] - 
    yu[ff1, ff2] QLbar[sp, ii, ff1, cc].uR [sp, ff2, cc] Phibar[jj] Eps[ii, jj], FlavorExpand -> SU2D];
  yuk = yuk /. { CKM[a_, b_] Conjugate[CKM[a_, c_]] -> IndexDelta[b, c], CKM[b_, a_] Conjugate[CKM[c_, a_]] -> IndexDelta[b, c]};
  yuk+HC[yuk]/.feynmangaugerules
 ];

LGhost := Block[{LGh1,LGhw,LGhs,LGhphi,mu, generators,gh,ghbar,Vectorize,phi1,phi2,togoldstones,doublet,doublet0},
  (* Pure gauge piece *) 	
  LGh1 = -ghBbar.del[DC[ghB,mu],mu];
  LGhw = -ghWibar[ii].del[DC[ghWi[ii],mu],mu];
  LGhs = -ghGbar[ii].del[DC[ghG[ii],mu],mu];

  (* Scalar pieces: see Peskin pages 739-742 *)
  (* phi1 and phi2 are the real degrees of freedom of GP *)
  (* Vectorize transforms a doublet in a vector in the phi-basis, i.e. the basis of real degrees of freedom *)
  gh    = {ghB, ghWi[1], ghWi[2], ghWi[3]};
  ghbar = {ghBbar, ghWibar[1], ghWibar[2], ghWibar[3]};
  generators = {-I/2 g1 IdentityMatrix[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[1], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[2], -I/2 gw PauliSigma[3]};
  doublet = Expand[{(-I phi1 - phi2)/Sqrt[2], Phi[2]} /. MR$Definitions /. vev -> 0]; 
  doublet0 = {0, vev/Sqrt[2]};
  Vectorize[{a_, b_}]:= Simplify[{Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[a]], Sqrt[2] Re[Expand[b]], Sqrt[2] Im[Expand[b]]}/.{Im[_]->0, Re[num_]->num}];
  togoldstones := {phi1 -> (GP + GPbar)/Sqrt[2], phi2 -> (-GP + GPbar)/(I Sqrt[2])};
  LGhphi=Plus@@Flatten[Table[-ghbar[[kkk]].gh[[lll]] Vectorize[generators[[kkk]].doublet0].Vectorize[generators[[lll]].(doublet+doublet0)],{kkk,4},{lll,4}]] /.togoldstones;

ExpandIndices[ LGhs + If[FeynmanGauge, LGh1 + LGhw + LGhphi,0], FlavorExpand->SU2W]];

LSM:= LGauge + LFermions + LHiggs + LYukawa + LGhost;

84: \abstract{We perform a global fit within the pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone dark matter (DM) model emerging from an additional complex scalar singlet with a softly broken global $U(1)$ symmetry.~Leading to a momentum-suppressed DM-nucleon cross section at tree level, the model provides a natural explanation for the null results from direct detection experiments. Our global fit combines constraints from perturbative unitarity, DM relic abundance, Higgs invisible decay, electroweak precision observables and latest Higgs searches at colliders. The results are presented in both frequentist and Bayesian statistical frameworks. Furthermore, post-processing our samples, we include the likelihood from gamma-ray observations of \emph{Fermi}-LAT dwarf spheroidal galaxies and compute the one-loop DM-nucleon cross section. We find two favoured regions characterised by their dominant annihilation channel: the Higgs funnel and annihilation into Higgs pairs. Both are compatible with current \emph{Fermi}-LAT observations, and furthermore, can fit the slight excess observed in four dwarfs in a mass range between about 30--300\,GeV. While the former region is hard to probe experimentally, the latter can partly be tested by current observations of cosmic-ray antiprotons as well as future gamma-ray observations.}
85: 
86: \keywords{Global fit, pNG DM, frequentist and Bayesian statistics, \emph{Fermi}-LAT dwarfs, DM-nucleon cross section.}

101: \section{Introduction}
102: The true particle nature of dark matter (DM) continues to remain a mystery despite a plethora of astrophysical/cosmological evidence to support its existence \cite{Bertone:2010zza}.~Although the well-known Weakly Interacting Massive Particle (WIMP) offers a viable solution, most common models are strongly constrained by direct detection experiments \cite{Akerib:2016vxi,Cui:2017nnn,Aprile:2018dbl}.~This has forced us to either seek alternate particle DM candidates (e.g., axions \cite{Peccei:1977hh,Peccei:1977ur,Weinberg:1977ma,Wilczek:1977pj}, sterile neutrinos \cite{Dodelson:1993je,Shi:1998km}) or explore new ways of saving the canonical `WIMP paradigm'. 
103: 
104: A natural way of achieving the latter is to suppress the DM-nucleon interaction at tree level. For instance, in certain particle DM models, some parameter combinations can lead to blind spots in direct detection experiments or even a suppression of the DM-nucleon coupling \cite{Han:2016qtc,Choudhury:2017lxb,Han:2018gej,Altmannshofer:2019wjb}.~Alternatively, the DM-nucleon couplings could vanish due to symmetries \cite{Xiang:2017yfs,Wang:2017sxx}.~More commonly, however, particle DM models with a pseudoscalar mediator \cite{Fan:2010gt,Fitzpatrick:2012ix,DelNobile:2013sia,Boehm:2014hva,Bauer:2017ota,Tunney:2017yfp} leads to a momentum-suppressed DM-nucleon cross section.~Thus, this class of models can naturally evade the strong limits from direct detection experiments.
105: 
106: A popular example in this regard is the pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone (pNG) DM~\cite{Barger:2008jx,Barger:2010yn,Barducci:2016fue,Gross:2017dan,Balkin:2018tma,Huitu:2018gbc}.~It can be realised by adding a complex scalar singlet with a softly broken global $U(1)$ symmetry to the Standard Model (SM) particle content \cite{Barger:2008jx,Barger:2010yn,Barducci:2016fue,Balkin:2018tma}.~Due to the soft symmetry breaking, the resulting Goldstone becomes massive, i.e., a pNG boson.~An additional $CP$ symmetry ensures the stability of the pNG boson, which serves as a viable DM candidate.~The Goldstone nature of the DM particle implies that the pNG DM-nucleon cross section is momentum-suppressed at tree-level~\cite{Barger:2010yn}.\footnote{In fact, this suppression persists in the general case of $N$ scalars which are symmetric under a global $U(1) \otimes S_N$ symmetry \cite{Karamitros:2019ewv}.}~Thus, a pNG DM model offers a natural way of evading the strong direct detection limits \cite{Barger:2008jx,Barger:2010yn,Gross:2017dan}. A leading-order contribution to the pNG DM-nucleon cross section in the zero-momentum limit appears at the one-loop level \cite{Azevedo:2018exj,Ishiwata:2018sdi}. For typical DM velocities in our galaxy, $v_\chi \sim 10^{-3}$, it can easily dominate over the tree-level contribution.~The one-loop cross section can vary by several orders of magnitude in the allowed model parameter space. It has been shown that for parameter points which satisfy the relic density constraint, the one-loop cross section is typically below $\sim 10^{-50}$~cm$^2$ \cite{Azevedo:2018exj} and thus beyond the expected reach of future direct detection experiments, e.g., LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) \cite{Akerib:2018lyp} and DARWIN \cite{Aalbers:2016jon}.
107: 
108: More recently, the pNG DM model was confronted against the constraints from perturbative unitarity, DM relic density, Higgs invisible decay, XENON1T, \fermi dwarf spheroidal (dSph) galaxies~\cite{Fermi-LAT:2016uux} and LHC searches at $\sqrt{s}$ = 13 TeV \cite{Azevedo:2018oxv,Alanne:2018zjm,Huitu:2018gbc,Jiang:2019soj,Ruhdorfer:2019utl}.~Projected limits from DARWIN were also imposed in ref.~\cite{Ishiwata:2018sdi}, although they were only slightly stronger than the perturbative unitarity constraint. The \fermi limits in ref.~\cite{Alanne:2018zjm} were computed in an approximate way by considering annihilation into $b\bar b$, (on-shell) $W^+ W^-$, $ZZ$ and $hh$, where the latter three channels were included by applying a re-scaling factor on the $b\bar b$ limit from refs.~\cite{Clark:2017fum,Boddy:2018qur}. In addition, the model has also been used as a testbed for fitting the galactic centre gamma-ray and cosmic-ray antiproton excess \cite{Cline:2019okt}.
109: 
110: The pNG DM model has also been studied in light of electroweak baryogenesis. In ref.~\cite{Kannike:2019wsn}, the authors found that the phase transition in this model is of second-order, and thus a sizable gravitational wave signal is not possible.~However, the situation definitely improves if the model is extended to possess a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ symmetry. In this case, both a strong first-order phase transition and a sizable gravitational wave signal is possible \cite{Kannike:2019mzk}.
111: 
112: In this paper, we perform a global fit of the pNG DM model.~Our likelihood include constraints from perturbative unitarity, DM relic abundance, Higgs invisible decay width, electroweak precision observables, and latest Higgs searches at colliders.~Our results are presented in both frequentist and Bayesian statistical frameworks.~We also post-process our samples by computing the gamma-ray flux and the resulting likelihood from \fermi observations of dwarf Spheroidal galaxies (dSphs). We consider a set of 41 and 45 dSphs, excluding and including, respectively, those that show slight excesses compatible with DM annihilation. We take into account all relevant annihilation channels including annihilation into $HH$ and $hH$ (where $h$ and $H$ are the 125\,GeV Higgs and new scalar, respectively) as well as those proceeding via off-shell vector bosons. In addition, we compute the one-loop pNG DM-nucleon cross section for our samples and compare the resulting values against  the current limits from XENON1T (2018), and projected future limits from LZ and DARWIN.~Our \feynrules \cite{Alloul:2013bka}, \textsf{UFO} \cite{Degrande:2011ua}, \textsf{CalcHEP} \cite{Belyaev:2012qa} and \textsf{FeynArts} \cite{Hahn:2000kx} model files are publicly available at the \feynrules database.\footnote{\url{https://feynrules.irmp.ucl.ac.be/wiki/pNG}}
113: 
114: The remainder of the paper is organised as follows.~In section~\ref{sec:model}, we introduce the pNG DM model. In section~\ref{sec:like_constraints}, we describe the various observables and likelihoods used in our global fit and in the post-processing.~Our numerical scan details, global fit results, including \fermi and direct detection constraints, are presented in section~\ref{sec:num_scans_results}.~We conclude in section~\ref{sec:conclusions}.~Appendices~\ref{app:dm-nucleon} and~\ref{app:oblique_pars} summarise analytic expressions used in this paper.

118: \section{Pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone Dark Matter}\label{sec:model}
119: We extend the SM Lagrangian by adding a new complex scalar field $S$ that couples to the SM particles via a \emph{Higgs portal} term, $\Phi^\dagger \Phi$ ($\Phi$ is the SM Higgs doublet).~The model Lagrangian is given by \cite{Gross:2017dan}
120: \begin{equation}
121: 	\lagr = \lagr_{\textnormal{SM}} + \lagr_S + \lagr_{\textnormal{soft}}, \label{eqn:mdl_lagr} 
122: \end{equation}
123: where $\lagr_{\textnormal{SM}}$ is the SM Lagrangian, 
124: \begin{align}	
125: 	\lagr_S &= (\partial_\mu S)^* (\partial^\mu S) + \frac{\mu_S^2}{2} |S|^2 - \lambda_{\Phi S}\,\Phi^\dagger \Phi |S|^2 - \frac{\lambda_S}{2} |S|^4, \label{eqn:S_part} \\
126: 	\lagr_{\textnormal{soft}} &= \frac{\mu_S'^{2}}{4} (S^2 + S^{*2}). \label{eqn:soft_part}
127: \end{align}
128: Notice that eq.~\eqref{eqn:S_part} is invariant under a dark $U(1)$ global symmetry:
129: \begin{equation}
130:     S \rightarrow e^{i\alpha} S,    
131: \end{equation}
132: where $\alpha$ is a real, space-time independent parameter.~However, the $\mu_S'^2$ term in eq.~\eqref{eqn:soft_part} softly breaks this symmetry.~Thus, the model contains a \emph{massive} Goldstone boson, i.e., a pNG boson.~After this symmetry breaking, we are left with a residual $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, $S \rightarrow -S$, of the dark $U(1)$ group, which forbids a linear term in $S$ in the above Lagrangians. 
133: 
134: The parameter $\mu_S'^2$ can be made real and positive by the phase redefinition of $S$.~Thus, eq.~\eqref{eqn:mdl_lagr} is invariant under a dark $CP$ symmetry:
135: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:CP_sym}
136:     S \rightarrow S^*.
137: \end{equation}
138: This symmetry is unbroken by the $S$ vacuum expectation value (VEV) as for positive $\mu_S'^2$, the VEV is real.~Thus, the total symmetry of the model Lagrangian is $\mathbb{Z}_2 \otimes CP$.
139: 
140: With an extra scalar, the scalar potential becomes
141: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:pot}
142: 	V = V_{\textnormal{SM}} + V_S + V_{\textnormal{soft}},
143: \end{equation}
144: where $V_S$ and $V_{\textnormal{soft}}$ can be read directly from eqs.~\eqref{eqn:S_part} and \eqref{eqn:soft_part} respectively. Meanwhile, the SM part of the potential reads
145: \begin{equation}
146: 	V_{\textnormal{SM}} = -\frac{\mu_\Phi^2}{2} \Phi^\dagger \Phi + \frac{\lambda_\Phi}{2} (\Phi^\dagger \Phi)^2.
147: \end{equation}
148: 
149: After electroweak symmetry breaking, the model spectrum can be analysed by decomposing $\Phi$ and $S$ in the unitary gauge as
150: \begin{equation}
151: 	\Phi = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
152: 	\begin{pmatrix}
153: 		0 \\
154: 		v_h + \phi
155: 	\end{pmatrix},
156: 	\quad S = \frac{v_s + s + i\chi}{\sqrt{2}},
157: \end{equation}
158: where $v_h$ is the SM Higgs VEV.~Under the dark $CP$ symmetry in eq.~\eqref{eqn:CP_sym}, $\chi \rightarrow -\chi$. This guarantees the stability of $\chi$ and makes it a viable DM candidate; the physical $\chi$ mass is $m_\chi^2 = \mu_S'^2$.
159: 
160: After imposing the stationary point conditions at $(\phi,\,s) = (0,\,0)$, we get
161: \begin{align}
162: 	\mu_\Phi^2 &= \lambda_\Phi v_h^2 + \lambda_{\Phi S} v_s^2, \\[1mm]
163: 	\mu_S^2 &= \lambda_S v_s^2 + \lambda_{\Phi S} v_h^2 - \mu_S'^2.
164: \end{align}
165: 
166: Given that the $S$ VEV is non-zero in general, the $\lambda_{\Phi S}$ term in eq.~\eqref{eqn:S_part} leads to a mixing between the $CP$-even interaction eigenstates $(\phi,\,s)$.~Thus, the squared mass matrix $\calM^2$ is non-diagonal, namely
167: \begin{equation}
168: 	\calM^2 = 
169: 	\begin{pmatrix}
170: 		\lambda_\Phi v_h^2 & \lambda_{\Phi S} v_h v_s \\[1.5mm]
171: 		\lambda_{\Phi S} v_h v_s & \lambda_S v_s^2
172: 	\end{pmatrix}.
173: \end{equation}
174: As $\calM^2$ is real and symmetric, it can be diagonalised by a unitary transformation:
175: \begin{equation}
176: 	 \mathcal{O}^T \calM^2 O = 
177: 	 \begin{pmatrix}
178: 	 	m_h^2 & 0 \\
179: 	 	0 & m_H^2
180: 	 \end{pmatrix},
181: \end{equation}
182: where 
183: \begin{equation}
184: 	\mathcal{O} = 
185: 	\begin{pmatrix}
186: 		 \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\
187: 		-\sin\theta & \cos\theta
188: 	\end{pmatrix}.
189: \end{equation}
190: Here $\theta$ is a mixing angle that satisfies the following relation:
191: \begin{equation}
192: 	\tan 2\theta = \frac{2 \lambda_{\Phi S} v_h v_s}{\lambda_S v_s^2 - \lambda_\Phi v_h^2}.
193: \end{equation}
194: The eigenvalues of $\calM^2$ correspond to the masses of the $CP$-even mass eigenstates $(h,\,H)$,
195: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:m1_m2}
196: 	m_{h,\,H}^{2} = \frac{1}{2} \left[\lambda_\Phi v_h^{2} + \lambda_{S} v_{s}^{2} \mp \left(\frac{\lambda_{S} v_{s}^{2} - \lambda_\Phi v_h^{2}}{\cos 2\theta} \right)\right]\;.
197: \end{equation}
198: Given the discovery of a SM-like Higgs at the LHC \cite{Aad:2012tfa,Chatrchyan:2012xdj}, we identify $h$ as a SM-like Higgs boson with
199: \begin{equation}
200: 	 m_h = 125\;\textnormal{GeV}, \quad v_h = 246
201: 	 \;\textnormal{GeV}.	
202: \end{equation}
203: Thus, the pNG DM model contains 4 free parameters:
204: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:free_pars}
205: 	\left\{ m_\chi, \, v_s, \, \theta, \, m_H \right\}.
206: \end{equation}
207: The remaining parameters in eqs.~\eqref{eqn:S_part} and \eqref{eqn:soft_part} can be expressed as
208: \begin{align}
209: 	\lambda_\Phi &= \frac{1}{v_h^2} \left(m_h^2 \cos^2 \theta + m_H^2 \sin^2 \theta \right), & \mu_S'^2 &= m_\chi^2, \label{eqn:dep-Pars-start} \\[1.2mm]
210: 	\lambda_S &= \frac{1}{v_s^2} \left(m_h^2 \sin^2 \theta + m_H^2 \cos^2 \theta \right), & \mu_\Phi^2 &= \lambda_\Phi v_h^2 + \lambda_{\Phi S} v_s^2, \label{eqn:lamS} \\[1.2mm]
211: 	\lambda_{\Phi S} &= \frac{1}{v_h v_s} \left(m_H^2 - m_h^2 \right) \sin \theta \cos \theta, & \mu_S^2 &= \lambda_{S} v_s^2 + \lambda_{\Phi S} v_h^2 - \mu_S'^2. \label{eqn:lamPS}
212: \end{align}

216: \section{Observables and constraints}\label{sec:like_constraints}
217: In this section, we describe the set of constraints included in our global fit and post-processing of final samples.
218: 
219: 
220: \subsection{Theoretical bounds}
221: We require the model parameters to satisfy the following two theoretical bounds.
222: \begin{enumerate}
223:     \item \emph{Bounded tree-level potential}: The tree-level potential in eq.~\eqref{eqn:pot} must be bounded from below. This translates into the following lower bounds:
224:     \begin{equation}
225:     	\lambda_\Phi > 0, \quad \lambda_S > 0, \quad \lambda_{\Phi S} > - \sqrt{\lambda_\Phi \lambda_S}.
226:     \end{equation}
227: 
228:     \item \emph{Perturbative unitarity}: We require the perturbative unitarity of scattering amplitudes \cite{Lee:1977lhj}.~Using the $HH \rightarrow HH$ scattering process, we impose the following upper bound on the $S$ quartic coupling \cite{Chen:2014ask}:
229:     \begin{equation}\label{eqn:pert_unit}
230:         \lambda_S < 8\pi/3.
231:     \end{equation}
232:     Although this bound can vary with the exact scattering process of interest, we choose this form to maintain comparability with previous studies in literature~\cite{Gross:2017dan,Ishiwata:2018sdi,Huitu:2018gbc,Cline:2019okt}.
233: \end{enumerate}
234: Parameter points that do not fulfill these requirements are discarded from our scan. This is formally achieved by assigning a very small likelihood to such points.
235: 
236: 
237: \subsection{Thermal relic abundance}
238: The pNG boson $\chi$ is the DM candidate. Similar to the extended scalar singlet model \cite{Beniwal:2018hyi}, $\chi$ can annihilate into $f\ovr{f}$ (where $f$ = quarks/leptons), $W^+ W^-$, $Z Z$, $hh$, $h H$ and $HH$ final states via an $s$-channel $h/H$ exchange. In addition, $\chi$ annihilation into $h h$, $hH$ and $HH$ final states is also possible via $t$- and $u$-channels via $\chi$ exchange.
239: 
240: In our numerical scans, we require $\chi$ to make up \emph{all} of the observed DM relic abundance.\footnote{In general, $\chi$ can account for a subdominant component of the observed DM relic abundance, i.e., $f_{\textnormal{rel}} \equiv \Omega_\chi/\Omega_{\textnormal{DM}} < 1$. However, this choice (generally) leads to a larger allowed parameter space than the $f_{\textnormal{rel}} = 1$ case \cite{Beniwal:2018hyi}. We adopt the latter choice in our study.}~This is achieved using a Gaussian likelihood function for the DM relic density that is centered at the \planck (2018) measured value \cite{Aghanim:2018eyx}:
241: \begin{equation}
242:     \Omega_{\textnormal{DM}} h^2 = 0.120 \pm 0.001.    
243: \end{equation}
244: We also include a 5\% theoretical uncertainty and combine it in quadrature with the \planck measured uncertainty. This is done to reflect any uncertainties arising from the relic density calculation in \micro \cite{Belanger:2018mqt}.
245: 
246: With two neutral scalar mediators, the $\chi$ annihilation cross section is resonantly enhanced when $m_\chi \sim m_{h,\,H}/2$. To obtain the correct DM abundance, the $\chi$ annihilation cross section must be sufficiently suppressed. This is achieved for small values of $v_h/v_s$ (or large $v_s$); an expression for the DM-scalar coupling can be found in appendix~\ref{app:dm-nucleon}. Away from these resonances, large values of $v_h/v_s$ (or small $v_s$) generally saturates the $\chi$ relic density to the observed value.
247: 
248: 
249: \subsection{Higgs invisible decay width}
250: When $m_\chi \lesssim m_{h,\,H}/2$, the two scalars $\{h,\,H\}$ are kinematically allowed to decay into a pair of DM particles, i.e., $h,\,H \rightarrow \chi\chi$. This contributes to the following invisible decay widths \cite{Huitu:2018gbc}: 
251: \begin{align}
252:     \Gamma_{\textnormal{inv}} (h \rightarrow \chi \chi) &= \frac{1}{32\pi} \frac{m_h^3 \sin^2\theta}{v_s^2} \sqrt{1 - \frac{4 m_\chi^2}{m_h^2}}, \\
253:     \Gamma_{\textnormal{inv}} (H \rightarrow \chi \chi) &= \frac{1}{32\pi} \frac{m_H^3 \cos^2\theta}{v_s^2} \sqrt{1 - \frac{4 m_\chi^2}{m_H^2}}.
254: \end{align}
255: 
256: Recently, both the ATLAS \cite{Aaboud:2019rtt} and CMS \cite{Sirunyan:2018owy} experiments released new upper limits on the Higgs invisible branching ratio $\mathcal{BR}(h \rightarrow \chi \chi)$ for a SM-like Higgs from a combination of Run 1 and 2 analyses.~Here we adopt the conservative upper limit from the ATLAS experiment \cite{Aaboud:2019rtt}, namely
257: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:Gamma_up_limit}
258:     \mathcal{BR}(h \rightarrow \chi \chi) \equiv \frac{\Gamma_{\textnormal{inv}} (h \rightarrow \chi \chi)}{\Gamma_h^{\textnormal{tot}} (m_h)} \leq 0.26,
259: \end{equation}
260: where $\Gamma_h^{\textnormal{tot}} (m_h)$ is the total decay width of $h$ into SM and non-SM final states.
261: 
262: In the following, we apply the limit in eq.~\eqref{eqn:Gamma_up_limit} only on the scalar $h$ whose mass is fixed at 125 GeV. This experimental limit is derived from Higgs production in association with a weak gauge boson or through vector boson fusion (VBF), and assuming a SM-like Higgs except for the fact that it can decay to a pair of invisible particles, e.g., DM. The experimental signatures are large missing energy with either a weak boson or a pair of jets. Thus, the invariant mass of the invisible particles is not measured, and the second scalar can contribute as well to these processes.~However, this contribution is small when the mixing angle is small as the production of the second (first) scalar is suppressed by a factor $\sin ^2 \theta$ ($\cos^2 \theta$) compared to the SM production rate. The production rate also varies with the mass of the scalar but this effect is small for a light scalar ($m_H\sim 100$\,GeV) in the most constraining channel, i.e.,~VBF, as the cuts on the invariant mass of the two jets ($m_{jj}>1$\,TeV) are already requiring a very large partonic center-of-mass energy.~As the second scalar mass increases, its production rate is further reduced.~To sum up, our approximation is only valid for small mixing angles and for $m_H\neq m_h$.~However, as we show in the results section, the mixing angle is allowed to be large and even maximal when the two scalars are degenerate, i.e., when $m_H\sim m_h = 125$\,GeV. In this case, both scalars contribute to the process and interfere quite strongly. The amplitude can be written as
263: \begin{equation}
264:     \mathcal{A} \propto \frac{\cos\theta\sin\theta}{v_s}\left(\frac{m_h^2}{p^2-m_h^2+im_h\Gamma_h^\text{tot} }-\frac{m_H^2}{p^2-m_H^2+i m_H \Gamma_H^\text{tot}}\right),
265:     \label{eq:amp}
266: \end{equation}
267: where $\Gamma_h^\text{tot}\,(\Gamma_H^\text{tot})$ are the total decay width of scalars $h\,(H)$. The amplitude for the production of the scalar is multiplied by a factor $\cos\theta$ ($\sin\theta$) compared to the SM due to the modification of the couplings between the gauge bosons and $h$ ($H$). The remaining factors, besides the propagators, are due to the couplings with the DM particle $\chi$ (see appendix~\ref{app:dm-nucleon}). The missing pre-factor in eq.~\eqref{eq:amp} depends only on pure SM couplings and its exact expression depends on the process considered.~The two terms in the brackets can cancel exactly for $\theta=\pi/4$ if the two masses are identical, as in that case, the two widths are also identical. Thus, these points are unconstrained experimentally but many of them would be excluded by applying blindly the constraints on the invisible decay width, which is the dominant channel for low values of $m_\chi$ and $v_s$. However, the correct re-interpretation of the invisible width constraint goes beyond the scope of this paper and thus is left as a future work.
268: 
269: The upper limit in eq.~\eqref{eqn:Gamma_up_limit} constrains the $m_\chi \lesssim m_h/2$ region where $\Gamma_{\textnormal{inv}} (h \rightarrow \chi\chi)$ can be sizeable. In our numerical scans, we use a one-sided Gaussian likelihood function that is centered at the above measured value for $\mathcal{BR}(h \rightarrow \chi \chi)$.~Similar to the relic density likelihood, we add a 5\% theoretical uncertainty from our calculation of $\mathcal{BR}(h \rightarrow \chi \chi)$ and combine it in quadrature with the (expected) branching ratio uncertainty of 0.07 \cite{Aaboud:2019rtt}.

272: \subsection{Electroweak precision observables}
273: The extra scalar $S$ contributes to the gauge boson self-energy diagrams. Its effect on the electroweak precision observables (EWPO) can be parametrised by the oblique parameters $S$, $T$ and $U$ \cite{Peskin:1990zt,Peskin:1991sw}. As $S$ is electrically neutral, only the $W$ and $Z$ boson self-energies are modified.
274: 
275: Given that only the real component of $S$ acquires a non-zero VEV, the pNG DM $\chi$ (imaginary component of $S$) does not contribute to the $W/Z$ self-energies.~Thus, the oblique parameters in our model have the same functional dependency as in the extended scalar singlet model \cite{Beniwal:2018hyi}, namely, 
276: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:mod_oblique}
277:     \Delta \mathcal{O} \equiv \mathcal{O} - \mathcal{O}_{\textnormal{SM}} = (1 - \cos^2 \theta) \Big[\mathcal{O}_{\textnormal{SM}}(m_H) - \mathcal{O}_{\textnormal{SM}}(m_h)\Big],
278: \end{equation}
279: where $\mathcal{O} \in (S,\,T,\,U)$; for the analytical expressions, see appendix~\ref{app:oblique_pars}. From eq.~\eqref{eqn:mod_oblique}, it is clear that for large $m_H$, $\theta \sim 0$ is required, whereas large mixing angles $\theta$ are allowed for $m_H \simeq m_h$ (see e.g., ref.~\cite{Robens:2015gla}).
280: 
281: Using the SM reference as $m_{h}^{\textnormal{ref}} = 125$\,GeV and $m_{t}^{\textnormal{ref}} = 172.5$\,GeV, a recent global electroweak fit obtains \cite{Haller:2018nnx}
282: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:STU_pars}
283:     \Delta S = 0.04 \pm 0.11, \quad \Delta T = 0.09 \pm 0.14, \quad \Delta U = -0.02 \pm 0.11,
284: \end{equation}
285: and the following correlation matrix:
286: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:corr_mat}
287:     \rho_{ij} = 
288:     \begin{pmatrix}
289:         1 & 0.92 & -0.68 \\
290:           0.92 & 1 & -0.87 \\
291:           -0.68 & -0.87 & 1\\        
292:     \end{pmatrix}.
293: \end{equation}
294: In our numerical scans, we use the following EWPO likelihood function \cite{Profumo:2014opa}:
295: \begin{equation}
296:     \ln \like_{\textnormal{EWPO}} = -\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,\,j} (\Delta \mathcal{O}_i - \ovr{\Delta \mathcal{O}}_i) \left(\Sigma^2 \right)_{ij}^{-1} (\Delta \mathcal{O}_j - \ovr{\Delta \mathcal{O}}_j),
297: \end{equation}
298: where $\ovr{\Delta \mathcal{O}}_i$ are the central values for the shifts in eq.~\eqref{eqn:STU_pars}, $\Sigma_{ij}^2 \equiv \sigma_i \rho_{ij} \sigma_j$ is the covariance matrix, $\rho_{ij}$ is the correlation matrix in eq.~\eqref{eqn:corr_mat} and $\sigma_i$ are the associated errors in eq.~\eqref{eqn:STU_pars}.

301: \subsection{Higgs searches at colliders}
302: In the narrow-width approximation, the signal strength $\mu_h$ for a SM-like Higgs $h$ \cite{Huitu:2018gbc} is
303: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:mu_H}
304:     \mu_h \equiv \sigma(p p \rightarrow h) \cdot \mathcal{BR} (h \rightarrow \textnormal{SM}).
305: \end{equation}
306: The inclusion of $H$ in our model leads to a universal suppression of couplings between $h$ and SM particles. Thus, the $h$ production cross section is
307: \begin{equation}
308:     \sigma (p p \rightarrow h) = \cos^2 \theta~ \sigma_{p p \rightarrow h}^{\textnormal{SM}} (m_h),
309: \end{equation}
310: where $\sigma_{p p \rightarrow h}^{\textnormal{SM}} (m_h)$ is the $h$ production cross section in the SM.~Similarly, the branching ratio of $h$ into SM particles is
311: \begin{equation}
312:     \mathcal{BR}(h \rightarrow \textnormal{SM}) \equiv \frac{\Gamma (h \rightarrow \textnormal{SM})}{\Gamma_h^{\textnormal{tot}}} = \frac{\cos^2 \theta ~ \Gamma_h^{\textnormal{SM}}(m_h)}{\cos^2 \theta ~ \Gamma_h^{\textnormal{SM}} (m_h) + \Gamma (h \rightarrow \chi \chi) + \Gamma (h \rightarrow HH) },
313: \end{equation}
314: where $\Gamma_h^{\textnormal{SM}} (m_h)$ is the total decay width of a SM-like Higgs $h$ with mass $m_h$ into SM final states.~The last two terms in the denominator correspond to the new decay modes of $h$, namely $h \rightarrow \chi \chi$ and $h \rightarrow HH$. 
315: 
316: Thus, the signal strength $\mu_h$ in eq.~\eqref{eqn:mu_H} becomes
317: \begin{equation}\label{eqn:mu_h}
318:     \mu_h = \frac{\cos^4 \theta ~ \mu_h^{\textnormal{SM}} }{\cos^2 \theta ~ \Gamma_h^{\textnormal{SM}}(m_h) + \Gamma (h \rightarrow \chi \chi) + \Gamma (h \rightarrow HH)},
319: \end{equation}
320: where $\mu_h^{\textnormal{SM}} \equiv \sigma_{p p \rightarrow h}^{\textnormal{SM}} (m_h) \cdot \Gamma_h^{\textnormal{SM}}(m_h)$ is the $h$ signal strength in the SM. From the above expression, it is clear that $\mu_h \neq \mu_h^{\textnormal{SM}}$ when the mixing angle $\theta \neq 0$, or when $h$ decay into non-SM final states  is kinematically allowed. 
321: 
322: To constrain the parameters of the pNG DM model in our scan, we take into account the following two contributions to the likelihood:
323: \begin{itemize}
324:     \item We consider Higgs searches performed at the LEP experiment by utilising the \HBver \cite{Bechtle:2019kbl,Bechtle:2013wla} package. It allows us to compute a $\chi^2_{\textnormal{LEP}}$ for the most-sensitive LEP analysis on the basis of the scalar masses, effective Higgs-SM couplings, total decay widths and branching ratios. The corresponding likelihood function reads:
325:     \begin{equation}
326:         \ln \like_{\textnormal{LEP}} = - \frac{1}{2} \chi^2_{\textnormal{LEP}}.
327:     \end{equation}
328:     \item We take into account constraints from the observed Higgs signal strengths and mass measurements performed for a SM-like Higgs at the LHC. This is achieved using the \HSver \cite{Bechtle:2013xfa} package. In practice, we compute three contributions to the $\chi^2$ that are based on \emph{i}) combined run 1 results $(\chi^2_{\textnormal{R1}})$; \emph{ii}) results from 13 TeV LHC analyses $(\chi^2_{\textnormal{13\,TeV}})$; and \emph{iii}) results in the form of Simplified Template Cross Sections (STXS) $(\chi^2_{\textnormal{STXS}})$. The final \HS likelihood that we use in our scans is
329:     \begin{equation}
330:         \ln \like_{\textnormal{HS}} = -\frac{1}{2} \left(\chi^2_{\textnormal{R1}} + \chi^2_{\textnormal{13\,TeV}} + \chi^2_{\textnormal{STXS}} \right).
331:     \end{equation}
332:     Each of the individual chi-squares are computed using the \emph{peak-centered} method with Gaussian probability density function and zero theoretical mass uncertainty for the two scalar masses. For more details, see ref.~\cite{Bechtle:2013xfa}.
333: \end{itemize}
334: The LEP analyses that we use are sensitive to parameter points with $m_H \lesssim 120$\,GeV only, whereas the observed Higgs signal strengths potentially constrain points with $m_H$ in the whole considered mass range.\footnote{Note that we do not consider constraints from direct searches for a second (heavy) Higgs performed at the LHC (also implemented in \HBver). Besides the technical limitation that \HB does not provide a likelihood for these searches, we found that the respective 95\% C.L. limits are weaker than those of other constraints applied in our analysis. In particular, the EWPO constraint excludes sizeable values of $\theta$ in the region $m_H\gtrsim 130\,$GeV.}

354: \subsection{\emph{Fermi}-LAT gamma-ray observations}\label{sec:FermiCon}
355: Gamma-ray observations of dSphs by \fermi provide robust limits on the DM annihilation flux.~To constrain our model, we use the publicly available energy-binned likelihood profiles\footnote{\url{https://www-glast.stanford.edu/pub_data/1203/}} from \fermi \cite{Fermi-LAT:2016uux}, as implemented in \textsf{MadDM v3.0}~\cite{Ambrogi:2018jqj}.~We consider the set of all 45 observed dSphs and use the measured $J$-factors based on spectroscopic observations~\cite{Fermi-LAT:2016uux} as adopted from ref.~\cite{Geringer-Sameth:2014yza}.~When measurements are not available, we use the values predicted from the distance scaling relationship with a nominal uncertainty of 0.6\,dex~\cite{Fermi-LAT:2016uux}. We profile over the $J$-factor of each dwarf galaxy according to its uncertainty and obtain a total likelihood function as described in ref.~\cite{Ackermann:2015zua}. 
356: 
357: The corresponding gamma-ray energy spectra are computed using \textsf{MadDM}, while showering and hadronisation is achieved using \textsf{Pythia v8.0}~\cite{Sjostrand:2014zea}.~We include all annihilation channels that contribute at least 1\% to the total DM annihilation rate today. In particular, besides the usual $2\to2$ processes in \textsf{MadDM}, we also include $2\to3$ annihilation processes, $\chi \chi \to V V^*$, where $V^{*}$ is an off-shell weak gauge boson. In addition, we include $2\to3$, $2\to4$, $2\to5$ and $2\to6$ processes such as $\chi \chi \to H h$, $H H$ where $H$ decays further into pairs of SM particles, including $V V^*$. The decay of all on-shell SM particles is performed within \textsf{Pythia}.
358: 
359: In four (Reticulum II, Tucana III, Tucana IV and Indus II) of the 45 dSphs, slight excesses have been found with a local significance of roughly $2\sigma$ each~\cite{Geringer-Sameth:2015lua,Li:2015kag,Fermi-LAT:2016uux}. Consequently, a combination of the likelihoods from all dwarfs favors a certain range of DM masses and annihilation cross sections that provide a flux compatible with the excess.~However, as the DM origin of these excesses is not yet established, we show our results in section~\ref{sec:num_scans_results} with and without including the respective four dwarfs.~The latter choice imposes an upper bound on the DM annihilation cross section only.
